Modulation of aggregation of silk fibroin by synergistic effect of the complex
of curcumin and β-cyclodextrin
Priyanka Dubeya, Pramit K. Chowdhuryb, Sourabh Ghosha,⁎
a Department of Textile Technology, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Hauz Khas, New Delhi 110016, India.

A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Silk fibroin
Curcumin
β-Cyclodextrin

Amyloidogenic aggregation
A B S T R A C T
Amyloid aggregation has been associated with numerous human pathological diseases. A recent study has de-
monstrated that silk fibroin intermittently endorses amyloidogenesis in vivo. In the current study, we explored
the propensity of silk fibroin to undergo amyloid-like aggregation and its prevention using an optimized con-
coction of curcumin with β-cyclodextrin. Aggregation of silk fibroin resulted in the formation of fibrils with a
diameter of ~3.2 nm. However, addition of the optimized concentration of curcumin and β-cyclodextrin to silk
fibroin inhibited aggregation and preserved the random coil conformation even under aggregation inducing
conditions, as demonstrated by CD and FTIR spectroscopy. Benzene rings of curcumin interact with the aromatic
residues of fibroin via hydrophobic interactions. However, β-cyclodextrin preferentially interacts with the non-
polar residues, which are the core components for nucleation dependent protein aggregation. The present study
demonstrates the ability of the concoction of curcumin and β-cyclodextrin in tuning the self assembly process of
fibroin. It also provides a platform to explore the assembly process of nano-fibril and hierarchical structures in
vitro along with a novel insight for designing clinically relevant silk-based functional biomaterials.
1. Introduction
The self-assembly/aggregation of proteins asserts different roles in
many of the regular physiological activities due to its specific structural
and functional properties, for example aggregation of explicit proteins
play an imperative role during blood coagulation and hemostasis [1].
On the other hand, anomalous protein assembly and aberrant ag-
gregation could lead to devastating disorders such as cancers, cystic
fibrosis, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and prion diseases [2]. Therefore,
requirement for a therapeutic agent for inhibiting the amyloid assembly
is of significant interest. A variety of small molecules have been ex-
plored to inhibit the protein aggregation [3,4]. However, the mechan-
isms for inhibiting the protein aggregation using small compounds are
still poorly understood, which results in slow development of new
therapeutics against amyloid pathogenesis. Thus, strategies for mod-
ulation of protein assembly would be of considerable interest in order to
address the aberrant aggregation. Furthermore, the controlled in-
vestigation of conformational transitions, fibrillation and inhibition of
aggregation of amyloidogenic proteins could shed light on the patho-
genesis as well. Such studies are however challenging due to aggrega-
tion propensity of amyloidogenic proteins, leading to lack of under-
standing in terms of reproducible kinetics data, limited evidence of
intermediate species, or amyloid fibril catalyzed secondary nucleation
mechanism [5].
The silk fibroin protein can be projected as a model protein to study
the inhibition of fibrillation due to a host of similarities between the
amyloid forming and fibroin proteins [4,6,7]. Moreover, studies fo-
cusing on self-assembly process of silk fibroin protein can not only
provide a platform to explore the assembly process from nano-fibril to
hierarchical structures in vitro, but also generate novel insights for de-
signing new silk-based functional biomaterials [8]. Recent reports in-
dicated that silk fibroin-based biomaterials occasionally promote
amyloidogenesis in vivo [9]. Another study showed that fibroin could
assemble into elongated fibrillar morphology comparable to amyloid
depending upon the processing conditions, concentration of fibroin and
concentration of ethanol [10]. Furthermore, treatment with less than
40% (v/v) of ethanol to the silk fibroin represents a nucleation de-
pendent fibrillation, which was not observed in case of higher con-
centration of ethanol [10,11]. Therefore, fibroin was used as model
protein to enhance our understanding of controlling the amyloidogen-
esis-like aggregation and to modulate its self assembly process.
Silk fibroin protein mainly consists of two distinct structural con-
formations namely, random coil, silk I (which is metastable, water-so-
luble, helix-like S-shaped zigzag/crankshaft or repeated β-turn type II

regions) [12,13]. Various factors such as shear, addition of ethanol
(alcohol), metallic ions and pH induce a structural transition from the
random coil structure to silk I to the β–sheet rich silk II structure during
the self assembly process [14–17]. Previously, we have illustrated that
optimized concentration of calcium ions can modulate the self-assembly
of random coil silk fibroin solution to β–sheet rich silk II conformation
through α-helical intermediates [18]. Moreover, the precise control of
self-assembly of fibroin protein can also be utilized for distinct im-
munological responses to silk biomaterial [8,18].
In the current study we have focused on controlling the aggregation
kinetics of silk fibroin in the presence of combination of two com-
pounds, curcumin and β-cyclodextrin. Addition of β-cyclodextrin and
curcumin has been reported previously to inhibit the aggregation of
protein partially or completely [7,19] and hence disfavouring the self-
assembly of protein into highly organized fibrillar structures. A bi-
phenolic compound, curcumin [(1,7-bis(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)-
1,6-heptadiene-3,5-dioene] is extracted from the roots of the Curcuma
longa [20]. It is a potent anti-inflammatory agent and also has some
remedial effects on Alzheimer's disease [21] due to its binding capacity
to amyloid fibrils [22]. Though curcumin has been widely accepted as a
chemotherapeutic agent, its limitations such as low bioavailability,
inadequate tissue absorption, poor solubility in water or physiological
pH medium [23,24], fast hydrolysis in alkaline medium and poor sta-
bility have been a major limitation towards its widespread usage [25].
Thus, it is essential to combine the curcumin with a carrier in order to
improve above-mentioned properties.
β-cyclodextrin belongs to another promising class of compounds
that have been used for modulating the self-assembly of proteins [19]
and inhibiting the amyloid fibril formation [26,27]. β-cyclodextrin is a
non toxic, cyclic oligomer consisting of seven D-glucopyranose units,
linked by α-1, 4 linkage and has been known to inhibit amyloid β-oli-
gomerization [19]. β-cyclodextrin has a hydrophilic exterior with a
hydrophobic cavity, which makes it an appropriate host for aromatic
guest molecules in water. Therefore, it may act as a carrier for curcumin
and thereby help overcome some of the aforementioned limitations of
the curcumin. In the current work, we have used this combination of
curcumin and β-cyclodextrin to induce controlled conformational
translation and fibrillation of the silk fibroin protein and prevent its
aggregation, which could potentially elucidate pathogenesis of amy-
loid-forming proteins. This study is also significant because the iden-
tification of secondary structural conformations that shed light on en-
abling the protein to remain as soluble and functional rather than in
aggregated form, has a noteworthy impact under physiological condi-
tions [8]. This study can further be explored to control the fibroin
protein conformations by precisely tuning its self assembly process for
designing and developing the advanced silk biomaterials for various
biomedical applications.

2.2. Docking of curcumin and β-cyclodextrin into N-terminal domain of silk
fibroin
Firstly we carried out the in silico molecular docking analysis of fi-
broin to predict the most stable complex structure between curcumin,
β-cyclodextrin and silk fibroin using PatchDock program (http://
bioinfo3d.cs.tau.ac.il/PatchDock/index.html) [28]. The N-terminal se-
quence of silk fibroin protein available in PDB (PDB id: 3UA0) was used
for the docking studies. PatchDock requires the receptor and ligand
molecules in PDB format and calculates the three-dimensional trans-
formations based on the geometry based docking algorithm. It segre-
gates the molecules into concave, convex and flat patches based on
Connolly dot surface Representation [28]. It further calculates the
complementary patch based on Geometric Hashing algorithm for three
dimensional transformations that evaluate the scoring function based
on both atomic desolvation energy and geometric fit. PatchDock re-
moves the redundant solutions using RMSD (root-mean-square devia-
tion) clustering.
2.3. Isolation of regenerated aqueous solution of fibroin from cocoons
Fibroin solution from Bombyx mori cocoons was obtained as re-
ported previously [18]. Degumming was carried out by boiling the
cocoons twice, for 20 min each in 0.02 M Na2CO3 to remove the sericin
protein. Fibers obtained after degumming were washed thoroughly
with ultrapure milli-Q water and kept for drying overnight. Further,
9.3 M LiBr was used to dissolve the fibers at 60 °C for 3–4 h. The re-
sulted protein solution was dialyzed using ultrapure milli-Q water for
48 h at 25 °C. The final concentration of regenerated fibroin solution
was 6 wt%.
2.4. Congo red (CR) dye preparation and binding assay
A 20 mM stock solution of CR was prepared in deionised water to
get the final concentration of 20 μM during experiments. The CR solu-
tion was filtered thrice with 0.2 μm filter. Absorbance was recorded at
540 nm after 75 min incubation at 25 °C using a spectrophotometer
(UV-2450, Shimadzu, Japan). CR was added 15 min prior to spectral
analysis in all the samples.
For studying the aggregation kinetics of fibroin with ethanol using
CR dye a 50 mg/ml stock solution of fibroin was diluted with deionised
water to obtain a final concentration of 1 mg/ml. Fibroin solution was
further incubated with different concentrations of ethanol (0, 5, 10, 20,
30, 40%) for 75 min at 25 °C. CR absorbance was recorded at 540 nm
for all the samples at regular time intervals from 0 to 75 min.
